title: Scaling and Scheduling Services
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of scaling and scheduling services.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to scaling and scheduling services.

content.intro: This lesson covers Scaling and Scheduling Services. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Swarm is Docker Engine’s optional cluster orchestration mode for services distributed across nodes. It is not required for ordinary Compose-based local development. Test cluster changes on an isolated environment and avoid exposing management ports or join tokens. Learning scaling and scheduling services helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
